claim: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are one of the most toxic forms of DNA lesions.
source: One such response is the repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), one of the most toxic forms of DNA lesions.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract and introduction, drawing on general scientific knowledge about DNA damage.

claim: In Escherichia coli, DSBs are repaired via RecBCD-dependent homologous recombination.
source: In Escherichia coli, DSBs are repaired via RecBCD-dependent homologous recombination.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about E. coli DNA repair mechanisms.

claim: RecBCD over-expression can lead to reduced DNA repair ability.
source: RecBCD is essential for accurate chromosome maintenance, but its over-expression can lead to reduced DNA repair ability.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work (Dermić et al., 2005) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: RecB is present in very low abundance at mRNA and protein levels.
source: Using single-molecule fluorescence microscopy, we have established that RecB is present in very low abundance at mRNA and protein levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-molecule fluorescence microscopy presented in the manuscript.

claim: RecB transcription shows high fluctuations.
source: RecB transcription shows high fluctuations, yet cell-to-cell protein variability remains remarkably low.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of mRNA distributions and coefficient of variation calculations.

claim: Cell-to-cell RecB protein variability remains remarkably low despite high transcriptional fluctuations.
source: RecB transcription shows high fluctuations, yet cell-to-cell protein variability remains remarkably low.
evidence: This is supported by experimental protein quantification data and comparison with theoretical predictions.

claim: Hfq binds to recB mRNA.
source: Here, we show that the post-transcriptional regulator Hfq binds to recB mRNA and downregulates RecB protein translation in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by CLASH data showing Hfq-binding sites on recB mRNA.

claim: Hfq downregulates RecB protein translation in vivo.
source: Here, we show that the post-transcriptional regulator Hfq binds to recB mRNA and downregulates RecB protein translation in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased RecB protein levels in Δhfq mutants.

claim: Specific disruption of the Hfq-binding site leads to more efficient translation of recB mRNAs.
source: Furthermore, specific disruption of the Hfq-binding site leads to more efficient translation of recB mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the recB-5'UTR* mutant showing increased translational efficiency.

claim: A less effective reduction of RecB protein fluctuations is observed in the absence of Hfq.
source: In addition, we observe a less effective reduction of RecB protein fluctuations in the absence of Hfq.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of coefficient of variation between wild-type and Δhfq strains.

claim: DSBs can lead to loss of genetic information if not repaired or repaired incorrectly.
source: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), simultaneous lesions on both strands of the chromosome, are one of the most detrimental types of DNA damage because they can lead to loss of genetic information.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the consequences of DSBs, supported by citation (Wyman and Kanaar, 2006).

claim: DSBs can trigger cell death, deleterious mutations and genomic rearrangements if not repaired or repaired incorrectly.
source: If not repaired or repaired incorrectly, DSBs can trigger cell death, deleterious mutations and genomic rearrangements (Wyman and Kanaar, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wyman and Kanaar, 2006.

claim: DSBs can occur during the normal cell cycle as a result of endogenous metabolic reactions and replication events.
source: In addition to various exogenous sources such as ionizing radiation, mechanical stresses and DNA-damaging agents, DSBs can occur during the normal cell cycle as a result of endogenous metabolic reactions and replication events (Mehta and Haber, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mehta and Haber, 2014.

claim: Spontaneous DSBs occur in 18% of wild-type Escherichia coli cells in each generation.
source: For instance, replication forks often encounter obstacles leading to fork reversal, accumulation of gaps that are repaired by the RecFOR pathway (Cox et al., 2000) or breakage which has been shown to result in spontaneous DSBs in 18% of wild-type Escherichia coli cells in each generation (Sinha et al., 2018), underscoring the crucial need to repair these breaks to ensure faithful DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sinha et al., 2018.

claim: RecBCD detects a double-strand DNA end and degrades both strands.
source: Initially, the multi-subunit nuclease/helicase enzyme RecBCD detects a double-strand DNA (dsDNA) end and degrades both strands.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about RecBCD function.

claim: RecBCD has been shown to process the chromosome for up to ∼100 kb at ∼1.6 kb/s in live bacteria.
source: Indeed, RecBCD has been shown to process the chromosome for up to ∼100 kb at ∼1.6 kb/s in live bacteria (Wiktor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wiktor et al., 2018.

claim: Chi recognition by RecBCD is probabilistic.
source: However, because this recognition is probabilistic (Cockram et al., 2015), RecBCD can degrade large chromosome fragments before DNA repair is initiated.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cockram et al., 2015.

claim: Overproduction of RecBCD has been shown to sensitize wild-type cells to ultraviolet and gamma irradiations.
source: As a result, overproduction of RecBCD has been shown to sensitize wild-type cells to ultraviolet and gamma irradiations (Dermić et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dermić et al., 2005.

claim: RecBCD expression is essential upon DSB induction.
source: In contrast, RecBCD expression is essential upon DSB induction (Emmerson, 1968; White et al., 2018), hence too low levels might impair DNA repair.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Emmerson, 1968 and White et al., 2018.

claim: RecBCD has been reported to be expressed at very low levels.
source: RecBCD has been reported to be expressed at very low levels (Hickson et al., 1985; Taylor and Smith, 1980) and is present in less than 10 molecules per cell (Lepore et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hickson et al., 1985, Taylor and Smith, 1980, and Lepore et al., 2019.

claim: RecBCD is present in less than 10 molecules per cell.
source: RecBCD has been reported to be expressed at very low levels (Hickson et al., 1985; Taylor and Smith, 1980) and is present in less than 10 molecules per cell (Lepore et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lepore et al., 2019.

claim: The ribosome-binding site of recB is located within the coding sequence of ptrA.
source: As sometimes found in bacterial operons (Oppenheim and Yanofsky, 1980; Schümperli et al., 1982), the ribosome-binding site (RBS) of recB is located within the coding sequence of ptrA, suggesting a potential translational coupling mechanism between these genes.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the genetic organization, with citations to similar examples in other operons.

claim: Previous attempts to explore RecBCD expression upon DNA-damage conditions did not reveal any transcriptional regulation.
source: Previous attempts to explore RecBCD expression upon DNA-damage conditions did not reveal any transcriptional regulation (Hickson et al., 1985; Hickson et al., 1984) and the recBCD genes were shown not to belong to the SOS-response regulon (Wade et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hickson et al., 1985, Hickson et al., 1984, and Wade et al., 2005.

claim: The recBCD genes do not belong to the SOS-response regulon.
source: Previous attempts to explore RecBCD expression upon DNA-damage conditions did not reveal any transcriptional regulation (Hickson et al., 1985; Hickson et al., 1984) and the recBCD genes were shown not to belong to the SOS-response regulon (Wade et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wade et al., 2005.

claim: RecBCD transcription is considered to be constitutive.
source: Thus, RecBCD transcription is considered to be constitutive.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from previous studies and is supported by the experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: The average level of recB transcripts is ∼0.62 molecules per cell in wild-type cells.
source: In wild-type cells, we detected a very low average level of recB transcripts: ∼0.62 molecules per cell.
evidence: This is supported by smFISH experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Approximately 70% of cells do not have any recB mRNAs.
source: Notably, ∼70% of cells did not have any recB mRNAs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The recB mRNA degradation rate is γm = 0.62 min−1.
source: By fitting the mean mRNA value evolution over time to an exponential function, we estimated the recB degradation rate as γm= 0.62 min−1 (CI95% [0.48, 0.75]) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from rifampicin time-course experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The recB mRNA lifetime is 1.6 min.
source: This corresponds to a recB mRNA lifetime of 1.6 min and is consistent with the genome-wide studies in E. coli where transcript lifetimes were shown to be on average ∼2.5 min across all mRNA species (Chen et al., 2015; Moffitt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is calculated from the degradation rate and is consistent with genome-wide studies cited.

claim: Transcript lifetimes in E. coli are on average ∼2.5 min across all mRNA species.
source: This corresponds to a recB mRNA lifetime of 1.6 min and is consistent with the genome-wide studies in E. coli where transcript lifetimes were shown to be on average ∼2.5 min across all mRNA species (Chen et al., 2015; Moffitt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015 and Moffitt et al., 2016.

claim: A twofold increase in recB mRNA abundance was observed within a narrow cell-size interval (∼3.0–3.5 µm2).
source: A twofold increase in mRNA abundance was observed within a narrow cell-size interval (∼3.0–3.5 µm2), which is consistent with an expected doubling of the transcriptional output as a result of the replication of the recB gene.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: recB transcription from sister chromosomes happens independently.
source: We further showed that recB transcription from sister chromosomes happens independently, in full agreement with the hypothesis of an unregulated gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and modeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The burst size for the recB gene is b ∼ 0.95.
source: We then inferred the burst size for the recB gene, b ∼ 0.95, and the rate of transcription, km = 0.21 min−1 (Supplementary file 1G, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is inferred from fitting experimental data to a stochastic model.

claim: The rate of recB transcription is km = 0.21 min−1.
source: We then inferred the burst size for the recB gene, b ∼ 0.95, and the rate of transcription, km = 0.21 min−1 (Supplementary file 1G, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is inferred from fitting experimental data to a stochastic model.

claim: The recB transcription rate is remarkably low and close to the lower bound reported range of transcription rates in E. coli (0.17–1.7 min−1).
source: The latter is remarkably low and close to the lower bound reported range of transcription rates in E. coli, 0.17–1.7 min−1 (Proshkin et al., 2010; Bremer and Dennis, 2008; Vogel and Jensen, 1994).
evidence: This is a comparison of the inferred rate with literature values, supported by citations.

claim: The average CVm2 in newborn cells was found to be CVm2 = 5.9.
source: The average CVm2 in newborn cells was found to be CVm2 = 5.9, almost twice larger than the lower bound given by a Poisson process (CV2Poisson = 1/〈m〉 = 3.1).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data.

claim: recB mRNA production is noisy.
source: This suggests that recB mRNA production is noisy and further supports the absence of a regulation mechanism at the level of mRNA synthesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the high coefficient of variation calculated from experimental data.

claim: The average RecB protein abundance is 3.9 ± 0.6 molecules per cell.
source: By applying this approach, we obtained RecB protein distributions for cells of all sizes and confirmed its low abundance: 3.9 ± 0.6 molecules per cell (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Halo-labelling experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The RecB protein removal rate is γp = 0.015 min-1.
source: The decay rate was extracted from the fit and resulted in γp = 0.015 min-1 (CI95% [0.011, 0.019]).
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase Halo-labelling experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: RecB protein is stable and effectively removed only as a result of dilution and molecule partitioning between daughter cells.
source: Comparison to the population growth rate in these conditions (0.017 min-1) suggests that RecB protein is stable and effectively removed only as a result of dilution and molecule partitioning between daughter cells.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the removal rate with the growth rate.

claim: The lifetime of RecB proteins is set by the doubling time.
source: This result is consistent with a recent high-throughput study on protein turnover rates in E. coli, where the lifetime of RecB proteins was shown to be set by the doubling time (Gupta et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gupta et al., 2024.

claim: The rate of recB translation is 0.15 min-1.
source: As discussed earlier, we focused on newborn cells and estimated the rate of translation as 0.15 min-1 (CI95% [0.12, 0.18], Supplementary file 1G, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is estimated from experimental data using the two-stage model.

claim: recB mRNAs are translated at low levels compared to other proteins in the cell.
source: This value fell below the lower bound of the previously reported range of the translation rates in E. coli (0.25–1 min-1) (Proshkin et al., 2010; Bremer and Dennis, 2008). Therefore, we concluded that recB mRNAs are translated at low levels compared to other proteins in the cell.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the estimated translation rate with literature values.

claim: The simulated protein distribution had larger fluctuations than the experimentally measured one.
source: Strikingly, the simulated distribution had larger fluctuations than the experimentally measured one (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of simulated and experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The standard deviation of protein numbers is higher in simulation (2.2) than in experiments (1.5).
source: While both protein means were equal because of the first-moment-based parameter estimation we used (Materials and methods), we found the standard deviations to be higher in simulation (2.2) than in experiments (1.5) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of simulated and experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The experimental coefficient of variation (CV2Data = 0.19 ± 0.06) is approximately half of the analytically predicted one (CV2Theory = 0.45).
source: We found that the experimental coefficient of variation (CV2Data = 0.19 ± 0.06) is approximately half of the analytically predicted one (CV2Theory = 0.45) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental data with theoretical predictions shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There is a potential regulatory mechanism of RecB expression that actively suppresses protein production variation.
source: This deviation from the theoretical prediction implies a potential regulatory mechanism of RecB expression that actively suppresses protein production variation to maintain protein levels within a certain range.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between experimental and theoretical noise levels.

claim: RecB protein concentration remained similar to the intact control under DNA damage conditions.
source: Under DNA damage conditions, RecB protein concentration remained similar to the intact control (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The average cellular RecB concentration is 2.28 mol/µm2 in perturbed condition and 2.12 mol/µm2 in intact cells.
source: In fact, the average cellular RecB concentration was surprisingly conserved: 2.28 mol/µm2 (CI95% [2.21, 2.32]) in perturbed condition and 2.12 mol/µm2 (CI95% [2.01, 2.32]) in intact cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Halo-labelling experiments.

claim: recB mRNA concentration is decreased under exposure to ciprofloxacin.
source: In contrast, recB mRNA concentration was found to be decreased under exposure to ciprofloxacin (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: mRNA concentrations under DNA damage conditions are ∼2.4-fold lower than in the unperturbed control.
source: Specifically, mRNA concentrations under DNA damage conditions are ∼2.4-fold lower than in the unperturbed control (Figure 3D: inset): 0.12 mol/µm2 (CI95% [0.06, 0.17]) upon DNA damage versus 0.28 mol/µm2 (CI95% [0.23, 0.32]) in the control.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The ratio between the average protein and mRNA concentrations in damaged cells is 19.7.
source: The ratio between the average protein and mRNA concentrations in damaged cells is 19.7 (CI95% [17.5, 24.2]) whereas it is 7.9 proteins/mRNA (CI95% [7.5, 8.3]) in intact cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A ∼2.5 increase in translational efficiency was detected under DSB damage conditions.
source: Thus, a ∼2.5 increase in translational efficiency was detected under DSB damage conditions (P-value <0.001, two sample t-test).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data and is statistically significant.

claim: There is decoupling between mRNA and protein production upon DNA damage.
source: Taken together, our results show decoupling between mRNA and protein production upon DNA damage, suggesting the existence of a post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism that controls RecB protein level.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of decreased mRNA but maintained protein levels.

claim: Hfq binding is mainly localized at two sites on recBCD transcripts: one in close proximity to the RBS of the ptrA gene, and the second further downstream in the coding sequence of the recB gene.
source: Analysis of the Hfq-binding profile across recBCD transcripts showed the interaction of Hfq with the recBCD mRNAs (Figure 4A). Hfq binding is mainly localized at two sites: one in close proximity to the RBS of the ptrA gene, and the second further downstream in the coding sequence of the recB gene.
evidence: This is supported by CLASH data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Multiple trinucleotide Hfq-binding motifs, A-R(A/G)-N(any nucleotide) were found ∼8 nucleotides upstream of the RBS of the ptrA sequence.
source: Interestingly, multiple trinucleotide Hfq-binding motifs, A-R(A/G)-N(any nucleotide) (Tree et al., 2014; Link et al., 2009) were found ∼8 nucleotides upstream of the RBS of the ptrA sequence (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Hfq may control translation initiation and/or decay of the operon mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of CLASH data and sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: RecB protein concentration in the Δhfq mutant is 2.67 mol/µm2 compared to 2.17 mol/µm2 in the control.
source: Quantification across five replicated experiments showed a statistically significant 30% increase in RecB protein concentration in the Δhfq strain (Figure 4C: inset). The concentration was 2.67 mol/µm2 (CI95% [2.54, 2.80]) in Δhfq compared to 2.17 mol/µm2 (CI95% [2.01, 2.32]) in the control.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Hfq binding to the recBCD mRNA does not substantially alter the stability of the transcript.
source: These results were confirmed by RT-qPCR measurements, which did not show any significant changes for recB mRNA steady-state levels and lifetime (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c and d). Thus, we conclude that Hfq binding to the recBCD mRNA does not substantially alter the stability of the transcript.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c and d.

claim: The average level of proteins produced per mRNA in the Δhfq mutant is 14.0, which is two-fold higher than in the wild-type cells.
source: The average level of proteins produced per mRNA in the Δhfq mutant is 14.0 (CI95% [13.0, 18.1]), which is two-fold higher than in the wild-type cells (P-value <0.05, two-sample t-test).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Hfq alters RecB translation in vivo.
source: Altogether, this demonstrates that Hfq alters RecB translation in vivo.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental observations of increased RecB protein levels without changes in mRNA levels in Δhfq.

claim: The noise suppression is less effective in the Δhfq mutant compared to wild-type.
source: As seen in Figure 4G, the wild-type strain shows effective noise suppression as the theoretically predicted noise is larger than the one detected experimentally. Interestingly, this suppression is less effective in the Δhfq mutant.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of noise levels shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Hfq affects RecB protein fluctuations.
source: This provides evidence that, in addition to the average RecB abundance, Hfq affects RecB protein fluctuations.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in noise suppression between wild-type and Δhfq mutant.

claim: RecB protein concentration was nearly fully recovered to the wild-type conditions after Hfq complementation: 2.57 mol/µm2.
source: Although in our experimental conditions, Hfq is expressed at lower levels than in wild-type cells (transcription is ∼ a third of the wild-type level, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), RecB protein concentration was nearly fully recovered to the wild-type conditions: 2.57 mol/µm2 (CI95% [2.50, 2.65]).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Hfq complementation impacts recB mRNA translation but not its stability.
source: We did not detect significant changes in the recB mRNA levels when expressing Hfq from the plasmid (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c), confirming that Hfq complementation impacts recB mRNA translation but not its stability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: A significant increase in RecB protein production was detected upon ChiX over-expression.
source: In contrast, a significant increase in RecB protein production was detected upon ChiX over-expression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When fewer Hfq molecules are available for RecB regulation because ChiX is overproduced, RecB is translated at a higher rate.
source: This suggests that when fewer Hfq molecules are available for RecB regulation because ChiX is overproduced, RecB is translated at a higher rate.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation of increased RecB protein upon ChiX overexpression.

claim: ChiX does not affect RecB translation directly.
source: To exclude the possibility of a direct ChiX involvement in RecB regulation, we characterized RecB expression in ΔchiX. No significant change relative to wild-type cells was detected in RecB mRNA or protein levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 3). Thus, we concluded that ChiX does not affect RecB translation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: A significant decrease in the concentration of mRNAs was detected in the recB-5′UTR* strain: 0.14 mol/µm2 compared to 0.28 mol/µm2 in the wild type.
source: We detected a significant decrease in the concentration of mRNAs in the strain with the modified sequence: 0.14 mol/µm2 (CI95% [0.07, 0.17]) compared to 0.28 mol/µm2 (CI95% [0.23, 0.32]) in the wild type.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Only a slight decrease in RecB protein concentration was detected in the recB-5′UTR* strain: 1.96 mol/µm2 compared to 2.17 mol/µm2 in the wild type.
source: Despite the mRNA steady-state level decreasing two-fold in the modified recB-5′UTR* strain, only a slight decrease in RecB protein concentration was detected in comparison with the wild type (Figure 5E): 1.96 mol/µm2 (CI95% [1.56, 2.36]) in recB-5′UTR* and 2.17 mol/µm2 (CI95% [2.01, 2.32]) in the wild type.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The RecB translational efficiency in the recB-5′UTR* strain is 16.3, significantly higher than in the wild-type cells (7.9 proteins/mRNA).
source: The resulting translational efficiency in the recB-5′UTR* strain was found to be significantly higher than in the wild-type cells: 16.3 (CI95% [14.3, 19.7]) in recB-5′UTR*, whereas it is 7.9 (CI95% [7.5, 8.3]) proteins/mRNA in the wild type (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The RecB translational efficiency in the recB-5′UTR* strain is comparable with the values observed in the Δhfq mutant.
source: Remarkably, the RecB translational efficiency in the recB-5′UTR* strain is comparable with the values observed in the Δhfq mutant (a two-sample t-test confirmed that the difference is not significant).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The translation of recB mRNA is limited by a specific interaction with Hfq.
source: Thus, when the main Hfq-binding site was deleted, the lower abundance of the mRNA was compensated by more efficient translation. This demonstrates that the translation of recB mRNA is limited by a specific interaction with Hfq.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental observations in the recB-5′UTR* mutant.

claim: This is the first experimental evidence of an RNA-binding protein involved in noise suppression in bacterial cells under native conditions.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first experimental evidence of an RNA-binding protein involved in noise suppression in bacterial cells under native conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding based on the experimental results presented.

claim: RecBCD overproduction led to less efficient repair when DSBs were induced using ciprofloxacin.
source: In agreement with a previous report (Dermić et al., 2005), we confirm that RecBCD overproduction led to less efficient repair when DSBs were induced using ciprofloxacin (Appendix 3—figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 3—figure 2 and citation to Dermić et al., 2005.

claim: Post-transcriptional regulation has been proposed theoretically as an effective strategy for reducing protein noise.
source: Post-transcriptional regulation has been proposed theoretically as an effective strategy for reducing protein noise (Swain, 2004; Shimoni et al., 2007; Singh, 2011; Bokes et al., 2021; Mehta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Suppression of protein fluctuations via post-transcriptional control has been demonstrated in synthetically engineered systems in bacteria, yeast and mammalian cells.
source: Based on these principles, suppression of protein fluctuations via post-transcriptional control has been demonstrated in synthetically engineered systems in bacteria, yeast and mammalian cells (Siciliano et al., 2013; Kelly et al., 2018; Mundt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies in synthetic systems.

claim: Suppressed fluctuations of protein expression were experimentally detected for hundreds of microRNA-regulated genes in mammalian cells.
source: Suppressed fluctuations of protein expression were experimentally detected for hundreds of microRNA-regulated genes in mammalian cells (Schmiedel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmiedel et al., 2015.

claim: microRNA-regulated genes with suppressed fluctuations were expressed at a very low level.
source: Remarkably, those genes were expressed at a very low level.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the cited study (Schmiedel et al., 2015).
